pages: Every village has a bell, and every bell has a job. Ours calls folk to market, warns of fire, marks a wedding, and counts the dead into the ground. I have rung it since my father's hands grew too stiff to climb the tower ladder, and in thirty-two years I have learned this: iron speaks plain, but it
does not always speak first.

There is a patch of belladonna behind the old sheep wall. No one planted it. No one admits to watering it. Yet every spring it comes up with leaves black-green and berries like buttons on a widow's coat. The children are told not to touch it. The goats know better without being told.
On the night Mistress Vale came to town, the belladonna bloomed out of season.

She arrived at dusk with a basket on one arm and a crow on the other, though I never saw the crow move. The baker's wife crossed herself. The reeve shut his shutters. I did what I always do when strangers come after dark: I rang the ninth bell and watched.

Mistress Vale did not ask for lodging. She bought a heel of bread, a twist of salt, and every brown egg left in the market. Then she went to the belladonna patch and knelt there like a woman at prayer.

By morning, little Piers was breathing again.

You will hear folk say it was fever turning on its own. You will hear the priest say Providence works through many hands. You will hear Piers' mother say nothing at all, because she knows how near she came to washing her boy for burial. I only know what I saw from the tower window: a witch at the

wall, a bowl of water gone silver in moonlight, three eggs cracked one by one, and her lips moving as if she were scolding someone too rude to answer.

After that, the village changed by inches.

People still spat when they said "witch," but they also left milk near the sheep wall when lambs came early. They still barred the doors on storm nights, but they asked Mistress Vale which shutters faced the wrong wind. The blacksmith swore no charm would ever hang in his forge, then tied a strip of

red thread over the bellows after his youngest stopped coughing.

I asked her once what the belladonna was for.

"Listening," she said.

"Plants do not listen."

"Neither do bells," she answered, "until someone teaches them what to carry."

I thought that was witch nonsense until the winter plague. Three graves in one week, and the fourth dug before the child had died. Mistress Vale climbed the tower with me then. She carried a sprig of belladonna wrapped in wool and told me to ring once, hard, when she gave the nod.

Below us, the village waited in the snow.

She tied the sprig to the clapper. She spoke to the bell, not loudly, but close, as if it were a stubborn horse. Then she nodded.

I rang.

The sound rolled over the roofs and went strange at the edge of hearing. Dogs whimpered. A flock of starlings burst from the church yews. Every candle in every window leaned toward the tower flame-first. When the sound faded, the snow kept falling, but the coughing in the sick house had stopped.

Not everyone lived. Witchery is not a bargain with kindness. It is not a rope thrown across every pit. It is a knowing of where the ropes are hidden, and what they cost to pull.

Mistress Vale left in spring. The belladonna stayed.

Now when I ring the dead into the ground, I listen after the last note. Sometimes there is only wind. Sometimes there is a hush that feels like a hand over a fevered brow. And sometimes, when the moon is thin and the berries shine, the bell answers back.

functions.title: Ashes in the Oven
functions.author: Elspeth Rook, witch of the south lane

pages:
The village thinks my work happens at midnight.

That is because the village sleeps at midnight and can safely imagine anything it likes. They picture knives, smoke, red circles, perhaps a skull polished bright enough to see tomorrow in. I do not blame them. Midnight has theater in it.
Most witchery happens after breakfast.

At dawn I clear the ash from the oven, and if the ash is pale I save it for chalk. If it is black and greasy, I throw it on the compost and call the fire lazy. I scrub jars. I sort roots. I argue with the kettle, which has opinions about rainwater. I mend the left cuff of my robe because the cat has

decided cuffs are prey. None of this would frighten a child unless the child had been raised to fear chores.

On market days, I trade cures for gossip.

Gossip is the best reagent. Breath of the Goddess can lift a fever, but only gossip tells you who was kissed behind the mill, who hides bruises under sleeves, whose cow dries up only when the new moon sits low. A witch who does not listen will spend her life making remedies for symptoms and never

once touch a cause.

Last Leafday, Mera Talbot came with a basket of onions and a lie.

"My husband cannot sleep," she said.

Her husband slept like a felled tree. Half the village had complained of his snoring.

I gave her tea anyway and watched her hands. They were red from lye. Her nails were bitten. Around her wrist she wore three turns of blue thread, tied by someone with clumsy fingers. A child's knot.

"Does your son dream?" I asked.

She looked at the floor. "He wakes screaming of antlers."

Ah.

Nightmares are not always dreams. Sometimes they are visitors too proud to knock. I packed mandrake, a scrap of wool, and one of my last clean jars. Mera tried to pay with onions. I took two because refusing payment makes folk nervous.

Her boy was seven, thin as a rake handle, with eyes too large for his face. His bed stood under a window that looked toward the forest. Above it, a toy horse hung by one thread, turning slowly though the room was still.

I sent Mera to boil water. Mothers need tasks when fear sits on their chests.

I placed a bowl under the window and poured in the mandrake steep. The smell could have shamed a pigsty. The boy laughed once, weakly, which told me he was not too far gone. I wound wool around the bedpost and pinned it with a thorn. Then I asked the room what it wanted.

The horse stopped turning.

There are two kinds of silence. One is empty. The other is listening.

"He is not yours," I told the corner.

The shadow by the window stretched itself into a shape like branches. I could have drawn a circle. I could have called fire. Instead I took the bowl and flung the mandrake water straight through it.

The scream broke three cups in the kitchen.

By sunset the boy was eating soup. By moonrise the blue thread around Mera's wrist had come loose on its own.

That night, the village saw my lamp burning late and decided I was whispering to devils.

I was washing jars.

The work is mostly jars.

functions.title: The Mayor's Black Cat
functions.author: Tollen Reed, clerk to Mayor Amabel Firth

pages: Before the cat, Mayor Firth was a sensible woman.

She kept accounts in straight columns. She salted roads before frost. She could hear a dishonest weight across a crowded market. If anyone had told me she would one day cancel a tax hearing because a black cat sneezed at the east window, I would have accused them of slander.

The cat arrived in the flour cart.

It was small, wet, furious, and covered in enough meal to look ghost-pale from nose to tail. The miller tried to throw it out. The cat bit him through his glove. Mayor Firth, who valued decisive creatures, wrapped it in her cloak and named it Ink.

At first Ink was only a cat. It slept in the ledger shelf, spilled sand across petitions, and placed dead mice on legal documents of which it disapproved. Then the strange accuracies began.

Ink hissed at Alderman Voss the morning before we found spoiled grain under his seal.

Ink slept on the northern map the day before the bridge washed out there.

Ink knocked a marriage license into the fire, and three days later the groom was discovered already married in Birchfall, Oakhollow, and possibly a hamlet no one could find on any map.

The mayor called it instinct. I called it office management.

Then came the witch trial.

Old Mother Hem was accused of souring milk, blighting cabbages, and making Jory Bell fall in love with the cooper's apprentice instead of the reeve's niece. The last charge was spoken softly, as if love were more embarrassing than blight.
The whole village packed the hall. Mother Hem stood alone in a brown shawl, looking less like a terror of the unseen arts and more like a woman who wanted to sit down. Mayor Firth asked for evidence.

They brought a cracked churn. A basket of curled cabbage leaves. A lock of hair tied with red thread. Jory Bell, red to the ears.

Ink sat on the mayor's desk, washing flour that had not existed for months from one paw.

The reeve spoke first and longest. He said the village had tolerated hedge ways too long. He said a line must be drawn. He said no honest woman needed charms.

At that, Ink stopped washing.

I saw Mayor Firth glance at the cat. I saw the cat look at the reeve's coat pocket.

"Empty your pocket," said the mayor.

The reeve laughed. Nobody else did.

Inside his pocket was a twist of waxed cloth. Inside that, a thumb-sized poppet stuffed with cabbage root and cow hair, bound around with red thread. Also a note in his own hand listing debts owed by the dairy families who had accused Mother Hem.

The hall went very quiet.

Mother Hem looked at the poppet and then at the reeve.

"Poor work," she said. "You tied the malice backward."

That was how we learned two things: the reeve was a thief, and Mother Hem was not nearly so harmless as she looked.

Afterward, Mayor Firth asked the old woman whether Ink was a familiar.

Mother Hem peered at the cat. Ink peered back.

"No," said the witch. "That cat is your conscience."

Since then, no one in the office signs anything until Ink has sat on it. The mayor says this is not superstition. It is procedure.

I have entered it in the ledger accordingly.

functions.title: The Price of a Clean Floor
functions.author: Mara Venn, apprentice witch

pages:
My mistress says a clean floor is the first circle.

I thought she meant it as a lesson in humility. Apprentices are always being handed humility in buckets. Sweep the floor, Mara. Scrub the jars, Mara. Pick the slugs off the wolfsbane, Mara. Do not ask the skull whether it is bored, Mara.

But the first time I drew a proper rite circle, I understood.

Dust lies.

You cannot see a broken chalk line under dust. You cannot tell whether ash fell from the brazier or someone tracked grave soil in from the yard. You cannot feel the floor's little slopes beneath your knees if crumbs from breakfast keep grinding into your palm. A dirty floor turns every working into

a guess, and guesses invite company.

That morning we were meant to call rain.

The fields had cracked open. Sheep nosed dry troughs. Even the well rope sounded thirsty. Men came to our door who had crossed the road to avoid it every other day of the year. They brought coins, cheese, a silver button, two apologies, and one threat carefully disguised as worry.

Mistress took the apologies and the cheese. She told them to keep the rest.

"Rain is not bought," she said. "It is reminded."

We spent an hour cleaning the floor.

I hated her for it. Outside, the village stared at our chimney as if smoke might hurry. Inside, I swept while Mistress sorted chalk by color and hummed that awful tune with only three notes.

When the floor was clean, she let me draw the outer ring.
My hand shook. Chalk dust gathered in the crease of my thumb. The circle wavered near the north point. Mistress said nothing. That was worse than scolding.

We set the offerings: water, wood ash, belladonna, a breath caught in a bottle, and one chicken feather because rain likes jokes. The kettle ticked over the fire. The room smelled of wet stone though there had been no wet stone for weeks.

Then the old skull on the shelf whispered, "Ant."

I froze.

Mistress looked at the floor.

One black ant crossed the chalk line.

It was tiny. It was absurd. It carried a crumb, which meant I had not swept under the table as well as I thought.

"Break," Mistress said.

I broke the circle with my sleeve, and the air snapped flat. Outside, someone groaned. Inside, Mistress picked up the ant on a scrap of paper and carried it to the garden.

"Again," she said.

"The village needs rain."

"The village needs us not to open a crooked door."

So I swept again. Under the table this time. Behind the stool. Beneath the rug I had pretended not to see. We drew the circle a second time. My hand did not shake as much.

When Mistress spoke the last word, the roof answered.

Not with thunder. Not at first. With one drop. Then five. Then such a drumming that the men outside shouted like boys. Water ran down the window in sheets. The dry yard became black mud.

Mistress handed me a mop.

"Now," she said, "you will learn the second circle."

I still sweep before every working. I sweep when no one asks. I sweep even when the floor looks clean. Especially then.

Witchery begins where pride ends.

There is rowan over my door, tied with red thread and my wife's hair.

I did not put it there. I came home from the north wood with frost in my beard and found the sprig fixed above the lintel. My first thought was thieves. My second was worse: witches.

My wife told me to leave it.

"It will keep out bad wishing," she said.

"Bad wishing has never paid rent here," I answered.

She looked at me in the way wives do when husbands have mistaken talking for thinking.

That winter, bad wishing came.

His name was Brennock, and he had once owned the strip of woodland I bought from his brother. He told everyone I cheated him, though the deed was signed and witnessed and paid in coin so heavy I still remember the ache of carrying it. Brennock smiled in public and spat when he passed my cart.

Then my axe heads began to crack.

Good iron, all of them. Split at the eye after a dozen strokes. My mule went lame without swelling. The milk soured. One morning I woke to find every nail in the woodshed bent like fishhooks.

My wife pointed at the rowan.

"Still there," she said.

The sprig above the door had blackened at the tips.

I went to Old Nan, who lives where the lane forgets itself. Folk call her a witch when they need someone blamed and Mistress Nan when they need a child turned from breech. She listened, chewing something that smelled like cloves.

"Do you want proof," she asked, "or peace?"

I said proof. I was younger then.

She gave me a rowan berry and told me to sleep with it under my tongue. I asked how I was meant not to choke. She said that was the first test.

That night I dreamed of my woodshed.

Brennock stood outside it with a twist of string and a chicken bone. He was crying. Not noble tears. Angry, ugly tears, like a man trying to wring water from a stone. He tied knots in the string and spoke my name between each one. Each knot became a bent nail. Each word struck the rowan over my door

and fell smoking to the ground.

When I woke, the berry under my tongue had turned to ash.

I went to Brennock's house with my axe.
I wish I could say I behaved wisely. I did not. I kicked his door open hard enough to crack it. He was at the table with the string in his hands. We stared at each other. Then he began to sob.

He said the woods had been his father's. He said his brother sold what should not have been sold. He said he had meant only to frighten me, not hurt my wife, not lame the mule, not spoil the milk.

I believed half of it.

Old Nan arrived before I decided which half. She had followed me, of course. Witches do that. They arrive exactly when men are most likely to become stories told as warnings.

She took the string, cut it once, and slapped Brennock so hard his chair tipped over.

"There," she said. "Justice."

"That is all?"

"No," said Nan. "Now comes repair."

Brennock fixed my shed. He paid for a new mule shoe. Every spring he brings my wife a rowan sprig, and she ties it over the door. We do not speak of the string.

The north wood is still mine. The grief is still his.
Witchery did not make that clean. It only stopped it poisoning the well.

My captain says a guard must count three things: doors, strangers, and candles.

Doors tell you who fears the night. Strangers tell you what the road is carrying. Candles tell you where trouble is awake.

On ordinary nights, our village has twelve late candles. The baker, because dough rises when it pleases. The priest, because guilt keeps poor hours. Two mothers with infants. One old man who sleeps by day and curses by moonlight. The rest are witches.

We have four, though only two admit it.

Mistress Jale keeps bees and sells salves. She admits to herbcraft, which is what witches call witchery when customers are listening. Young Corvin charms locks, shoes horses, and insists he is merely good with small mechanisms. No lock has ever agreed. The third is a girl of thirteen who makes

rainwater turn blue when she is angry. The fourth is my captain.

He thinks no one knows.

Captain Oren wears iron at his throat and keeps rowan berries in his boot. He can smell poppet work the way dogs smell meat. Once, when a traveling merchant tried to sell love philters by the well, the captain bought one, poured it onto the ground, and the dust crawled away from it in every

direction.

"Bad sugar," he said.

The merchant left before sunset.

One fog-month night, I counted nineteen candles.

Too many.

The extra lights burned in houses where no one should have been awake. The tanner's empty loft. The old granary. Three windows in the abandoned cooperage. A steady yellow dot under the bridge.

I woke the captain.
He did not ask questions. He took his spear, a pouch of salt, and the little brass bell he pretends is for signaling patrols. We went first to the bridge.

Under it sat seven villagers in their nightclothes, each holding a candle, each staring at the stream. Their feet were in the water. Their faces were peaceful in a way I did not like.

On the far bank stood something wearing antlers.

Not a deer. Not a man. It was too tall for one and too still for the other. The fog around it bent inward, as if listening.

The captain rang his brass bell.

The sound was tiny. Embarrassingly tiny. I nearly laughed. Then every candle went out.

The villagers woke screaming. The antlered thing turned its head. Where its face should have been, there was only more fog.

"Salt," said the captain.

I threw the pouch. My hands were shaking, so most of it went wide. Enough struck the water. The stream flashed white, and the thing on the far bank stepped back like a cat from flame.

Mistress Jale arrived with her bees.

I do not mean she brought a hive. I mean the fog filled with bees, hundreds of them, each glowing faintly gold. They made a wall between us and the antlers. The girl of thirteen stood behind Jale in her nightdress, crying angry blue tears into a jar. Corvin was there too, locking and unlocking his

empty hands.

The captain looked at them all and sighed.

"Nobody admit anything," he said.

By dawn the fog was ordinary again. The villagers remembered bad dreams. The bridge smelled of honey and salt.

Now I count candles twice.

Doors, strangers, candles. And if the captain's candle burns after midnight, I let it be. A village needs guards for the roads.

For the other roads, it needs witches.

functions.title: Lessons in Mutandis
functions.author: Brindle Thatch, hedge witch and bad teacher

pages:
My first apprentice turned a cabbage into a frog.

Not with skill. With panic.

Mutandis is change persuaded into a bottle. It is not meant for vegetables already committed to soup. I had told Nib to test it on grass, as any sensible witch does. Grass is forgiving. Grass has no ambitions beyond becoming taller grass or occasionally a flower.

Nib saw a cabbage, saw me looking away, and decided destiny had roots.

The frog looked as surprised as the cabbage would have, had cabbages faces.

"Can we change it back?" Nib whispered.

"Do you know the cabbage's true name?"

"It had a name?"

"Everything has a name. Most things are wise enough not to tell us."

The frog burped. A cabbage leaf came out.

Teaching witchery is mostly teaching restraint. Young folk think power is what happens when the world obeys. They learn, slowly and with many stains, that power is what happens when you know what not to ask.

The village does not see this. They see Nib walking with a basket of jars and think, there goes a witchling, half dangerous and half daft. They are correct, but not in the way they mean.

On the third day of lessons, I gave Nib a task: gather mandrake root without waking the plant.

"How?"

"Carefully."

Carefully lasted six minutes.

The mandrake came out shrieking, all legs and outrage, and Nib chased it through three gardens, over the baker's pig, and into the chapel, where it hid beneath a pew and made the priest forget the second half of his sermon. Earmuffs saved us from the worst of it. Pride did not.

That evening, while Nib sulked, I brewed Mutandis. Wood ash for memory. Mandrake for stubbornness. Egg for what may yet be. Bone meal for the promise bodies make to soil. Green dye because change likes a door painted its own color.

Nib watched the cauldron breathe.

"Is that all witchery is?" they asked. "Things becoming other things?"

"No. That is childhood."

"What is adulthood?"

"Knowing what they were before you touched them."

Weeks passed. Nib learned to grow rowan from saplings, to leave berries for birds, to ask water artichoke politely where it wished to root. They learned that belladonna is not wicked, only particular. They learned snowbell prefers cold fingers and that wolfsbane should be handled with respect even

when it looks harmless.

At midsummer, the miller's daughter came to us with a broken charm. It had been meant to keep nightmares out. Instead it kept sleep away entirely. Her eyes were bruised purple from waking.

Nib took the charm, sniffed it, and did not reach for Mutandis.

"This should not be changed," they said. "It should be untied."

Good.

We sat all night picking knots from red thread. At dawn the girl slept in my chair with sunlight on her face. Nib covered her with a shawl and looked at me as if expecting praise.

I gave them the frog.

It had been living happily in the herb trough, round and green and increasingly cabbage-scented.

"Find its name," I said, "and ask what it wants."

Two days later, we had a cabbage again.

Mostly.

It croaks when it rains, but many of us do.

I have delivered eighty-three children, six foals, two calves, one baby in a thunderstorm under a cart, and one witch's secret.

The secret came wrapped in a mirror.

It belonged to Selene Ash, who lived alone beyond the alder stand and came to births only when invited twice. Once meant the mother was afraid of gossip. Twice meant the child was in danger. Selene never took offense at being asked late. Witches are used to thresholds.

When Lysa Fen went into labor, the baby turned wrong. I tried all I knew. Warm cloth. Walking. Prayer. Threats directed at the father, who had fainted into the flour bin. Nothing.

So I sent for Selene twice.

She arrived with a mirror no larger than a plate, its frame blackened silver. She placed it under the bed.

"That is not clean," I said.

"Neither is birth."

Fair.

The room changed after the mirror went down. Not in a way any man would notice. Men notice blood, shouting, broken furniture. Women notice when air stops leaving through the cracks. The candle flames shortened. The shadows gathered under the bed like skirts.

Selene knelt beside Lysa and spoke to the child.

Not to the mother. To the child.

"Wrong door," she said gently. "Turn around."

Lysa screamed. I took her hand. Selene put one palm flat on the floor above the mirror. For a moment, I saw another room inside the glass: the same bed, the same candle, the same women, but all of us pale as moon milk and looking the other way.

Something on that side put its palm against Selene's.

The child turned.

He came into the world blue, furious, and alive. His first cry cracked the mirror from rim to rim.

Afterward, when Lysa slept and the father had been revived with vinegar, I found Selene in the yard burying the pieces.

"What was on the other side?" I asked.

"A possibility."

"That is not an answer."

"Most true things are not answers."

I disliked her for that. I disliked her more because I understood.

Years passed. I saw Selene's mirror work only twice again. Once for a boy whose fever showed him walking into a river before he had learned to stand. Once for an old woman who wished to see her dead husband and instead saw the daughter she had never forgiven waiting beside him.

Witch mirrors are not for vanity. They are for crossroads too narrow to stand on.

When Selene died, no priest would take the body at first. The village remembered too many cracked mirrors and not enough saved children. So I washed her myself.

Under her bed I found a bundle of mirror shards, each wrapped in linen and labeled in her thin hand.

Lysa Fen's son. Fever boy. Old Mara's forgiveness. Broken oath at mill. Lost cow returned. Midwife, if needed.

The last shard was whole enough to show one eye when I lifted it.

I am an old woman now. My hands ache in rain. I cannot run for witches in the night as I once did. The shard sits in my birthing bag between scissors and cord.

I have not used it.

But I have felt it grow warm twice, and both times a child turned before I asked.

functions.title: The Bargain at the Silver Vat
functions.author: Odran Kel, journeyman smith

pages:
Silver is an honest metal until witches touch it.

Iron tells you what it is. Copper complains but behaves. Gold is soft, vain, and useful for making rich men poorer. Silver watches. Leave it by the forge overnight and it looks back at you in the morning as if it knows what you dreamed.

The silver vat in Mistress Iven's shed was worse.

It crouched on three legs like a black kettle that had learned suspicion. Inside, a skin of metal shivered though there was no heat under it. I had come to repair a cracked handle, and I told myself I would not ask questions.

"Do not lean over it," Mistress Iven said.

So naturally I leaned over it.

The surface showed my face older by twenty years, with a scar I did not have and grief sitting under my eyes like soot.

I stepped back.

"Vat does that," she said.

"Shows the future?"

"Shows one bill you may have to pay."

I decided the handle could remain cracked.

She laughed and gave me tea strong enough to tan leather. We sat while the vat whispered tiny metallic sounds behind us. I asked what it was for, because smiths are weak before mysteries with hinges.

"Deposits," she said.

"Of silver?"

"Of consequence."

That was witch talk, which means true and annoying.

She showed me by dropping in a gold ring. Not much of a ring. Thin, bent, set with a dull red glass stone. The vat swallowed it without a splash. A moment later, three silver flecks rose to the surface, bright as stars in mud.

"A widow gave me that," Mistress Iven said. "Her husband promised it was ruby. He lied about many things."

"The vat punishes lies?"

"No. It renders them useful."

I thought of every false weight I had repaired, every sword sold as battle steel that would fold at first fear, every pretty hinge hiding rotten wood. The world was full of lies. We should have been rich in silver.

Then Mistress Iven asked why I had really come.

I showed her the knife.

It was my brother's. He had been bitten on the road east of town. The wound was not healing. It smoked at sunrise. He laughed at prayers and flinched from garlic though he had eaten it raw since boyhood.

"I need silver that hurts monsters," I said.

"Most monsters are hurt by truth first."

"I do not need a proverb. I need a blade."

She took the knife, weighed it, and looked at me for a long time.

"What will you give?"

"Coin."

"Coin buys metal. Not mercy."

So I gave what I had: the truth that my brother had not been bitten by a stranger. He had gone seeking the pale woman under the bridge because he wanted power. He came home changed, and I wanted him saved without anyone knowing what he had chosen.

The vat began to tremble.

Mistress Iven dropped the knife in.

When it rose, the edge shone silver-white. The handle was colder than winter. My reflection in it looked younger than I was, which frightened me more than the older face had.

"Cut the lie first," she said. "Then cut only if you must."

I went home and told my brother I knew.

He wept until dawn.

The blade stayed sheathed.

He still avoids garlic. He still watches the sunset like a thirsty man watches a cup. But he has not gone back to the bridge.

I repaired the vat handle the next week.

I did not lean over it.

functions.title: When the Broom Came Home
functions.author: Nettie Vale, witch of no fixed roof

pages:
A broom is not a horse.

This is the first lesson and the one no one believes until they are upside down in a hawthorn hedge.

Horses want oats, patience, and the illusion that they chose your direction. Brooms want balance, wind, and a rider who does not lie to herself. If you are afraid, the broom knows. If you are proud, the broom knows sooner. If you have eaten too much onion soup before flying, the broom will make its

opinion plain.

Mine was named Lark.

I did not name it. Never name a broom before its first storm. Names given in calm weather are decorative and usually wrong. Lark earned its name by rising through a thunderhead with such rude joy that lightning turned aside out of embarrassment.

We lived mostly between villages. I traded weather readings, curse untangling, and the occasional discreet truth for bread and thread. Some witches keep cottages. I kept a saddlebag, three jars, and a broom that stole ribbons from washing lines.

One autumn, Lark threw me.

Not far. Into a pond. Still, betrayal has no minimum distance.

I surfaced with duckweed in my hair and saw the broom hovering over the water, bristles twitching toward the east.

"Absolutely not," I said.

It dipped once.

East meant home, though I had not called it that in years. East meant Whitethorn. East meant a bell tower, a sheep wall, and people who remembered me as a barefoot girl who talked to nettles. I had left before they could decide whether that was charming or dangerous.

Lark flew east without me.
I followed on foot, wet, furious, and increasingly certain the broom had been right.

Whitethorn smelled smaller than memory. Smoke, apples, damp wool. The bell tower leaned a little more. The sheep wall had been repaired with mismatched stones. Above one cottage door hung rowan, fresh and carefully tied.

At the square, I found half the village gathered around a girl floating six inches above the well.

She was perhaps twelve. Her braids stood out as if underwater. Her mother cried. The priest prayed. The reeve suggested ropes. My broom hovered beside the girl, smug as a cat with cream.

"How long?" I asked.

The mother stared. "Since dawn."

"Angry?"

"Very."

"Good. Anger has handles."

I stepped close. The girl looked at me with eyes bright enough to scorch.

"They want me to stop," she said.

"Do you?"

That confused her.

Witchery often begins with someone else wanting you to stop.

I asked what happened. She said the baker's son had called her mother a hedge hag. She said the well rope snapped when she shouted. She said the ground forgot her afterward.

"The ground did not forget," I told her. "You let go first."

She began to cry then, and slowly, carefully, she came down. The moment her shoes touched stone, the well coughed up a silver fish no one had ever seen before.

The village gasped.

Lark knocked me in the back of the head with its handle.

So I stayed.

Not forever. Witches should be careful with forever. But long enough to teach the girl how to sweep a floor before drawing chalk, how to thank rowan without plucking it bare, how to listen when water turns quiet. Long enough for the village to stop whispering every time a jar clinked in my bag.

On the day I left again, the girl stood in the lane holding Lark's newest stolen ribbon.

"Will my broom come back for me too?" she asked.

"Only if it has better sense than you."

She smiled. That was answer enough.

Lark rose under me, eager for weather. Below, Whitethorn grew small. Not gone. Never gone.

A broom is not a horse. A village is not a cage. And home, if witchery has touched it, is rarely where you left it.

functions.title: The Mandrake at Millrow
functions.author: Oswin Hale, witness of Millrow field

pages: I was there when Tom Brindle pulled the mandrake.

That is the first thing I want written plain. I did not hear it from a cousin or gather it from alehouse talk. I stood three rows away with mud on my boots and a sack of barley seed over one shoulder. I saw his hands close around the green tuft. I heard him laugh before the root came loose. I heard

what happened after.

Tom had always been quick to laugh at warnings.

Old Mother Hem told us mandrakes were not weeds. She said if one grew among your crop, you marked the place, fetched earmuffs if you had them, and pulled after dusk with care. Tom said witches made rules so honest folk would feel foolish buying them charms.

"It is a turnip with a temper," he said.

The plant stood at the edge of Millrow field, between barley and the ditch. Its leaves were broad and dark, too clean for that muddy place. Even before the pulling, there was something mean about the stillness around it. No flies settled there. The wind moved the barley, but the mandrake leaves did

not stir.

I told Tom to leave it.

He grinned at me. "If it screams, Hale, I will apologize to the turnip."

Then he bent down and pulled.

The earth split with a wet sound. A pale root came free, twisted like a little person caught in a bad dream. It had thin limbs, a knotted head, and a mouth opening wider than any root should have a mouth. For one heartbeat the whole field seemed to lean toward it.

Then it screamed.

I dropped the barley. Someone behind me fell. The sound was not loud in the way a bell is loud. It was inside the teeth. It climbed through bone and made every thought in my skull scatter like spilled nails. I could see Tom shouting, but I could not hear him over the root in his hands.

The horses at the lane reared hard enough to snap a rail. Windows rattled in the mill. My left ear bled. A woman by the ditch began laughing and could not stop.

Tom tried to throw the mandrake away.

That was when it kicked him.

I swear this by every saint who ever looked away from us: the root kicked him in the chest with both little feet. Tom went backward into the barley, and the mandrake landed on the ground running. Not crawling. Running. It went straight for the ditch, shrieking all the while, legs flashing pale under

the leaves.

Panic makes scholars of no one. Half the field ran from it. The other half ran after it. I did both in that order.

Mother Hem arrived before the mandrake reached the water.

No one had sent for her. Witches are like rain on washing day; they come when your plans are worst. She wore earmuffs made of brown wool and carried a sack that wriggled at the seams. She stepped into the ditch path, planted both feet, and waited.

The mandrake saw her and screamed louder.

Mother Hem did not flinch. She opened the sack with one hand and snapped her fingers with the other. The root ran at her like a furious child. At the last moment she tipped the sack low. The mandrake rushed in, and she tied it shut with red thread so fast it looked like one motion.

The screaming became muffled. Then sulky.

Tom sat up, clutching his chest. "I think it broke something."

"Your pride, if we are lucky," Mother Hem said.

She gave the rest of us strips of wool soaked in something bitter and told us to press them to our ears. By sunset the laughing woman had stopped laughing. The horses settled. The mill windows held. Tom lived, though he claimed for a week that the mandrake had cursed his ribs specifically.

Mother Hem planted the root again beyond the hedge, under a marker of rowan twigs.

"Why not kill it?" I asked.

She looked at me as if I had suggested burning down the mill because flour makes dust.

"Mandrake is medicine," she said. "Also trouble. Most useful things are both."

Now, when I see those dark leaves in a field, I mark the place and fetch someone wiser. I do not laugh at warnings. I do not call roots by names they have not given me.

And if Tom Brindle tells you he pulled the mandrake bravely, ask him why he still wears wool in his ears every planting season.

functions.title: The Knots on Widow Fen's Door
functions.author: Captain Oren Vale, village guard

pages:
Report filed under weather, theft, and matters I am not admitting are witchcraft.

On the third morning of rain, Fletcher Dobb came to the guardhouse to complain that Widow Fen had stolen the wind.

I asked him how one steals wind. He said by tying knots in string, which was not an answer, but was at least more specific than most complaints made before breakfast. Dobb claimed the smoke from his chimney had blown backward for two days, his hens refused to lay, and every shirt on his washing line

had twisted itself into a rope pointing at the widow's cottage.

The reeve told me to investigate quietly.

The reeve says this whenever he wants a loud thing done by someone else.

Widow Fen lives at the north edge, where the palisade stops pretending it is a wall and becomes several hopeful logs. Her cottage is small, tidy, and watched by three cats who looked disappointed to see me alive. Over the door hung a length of red cord tied with nine knots. Feathers, rowan berries,

and a chicken bone dangled between them.

I knocked.

The cord moved though there was no wind.

Widow Fen opened the door with flour on her cheek and a knife in her hand. She is seventy if she is a day, thin as a fence stake, and has the calm expression of someone who has already decided where your body would be easiest to bury.

"Captain," she said. "Come about the wind?"

"Come about theft."

"Then you are early. It has not stolen anything important yet."

This is why people dislike talking to witches. They answer the question hiding behind the question, and then expect you to keep up.

I asked about the knots.

She looked past me toward the fields. "First knot for rain. Second for smoke. Third for stray teeth. Fourth for hoof-rot. Fifth for things that knock with no hands. The rest are none of your business."
I wrote that down because a guard should record confessions even when he does not understand them.

While I stood there, Dobb's boy came running up the lane, white-faced and breathless. Something had taken a lamb from the north fold. Not killed it. Taken it. The mud showed no wolf tracks, no boot marks, no drag. Only three round prints as if a stool had walked away carrying supper.

Widow Fen shut her door, untied the seventh knot, and handed me the cord.

"Hold this," she said. "Do not drop it unless you want to meet the stool."

We went to the fold.

The sheep huddled in the corner, all staring at the palisade gap. Beyond it, the rain fell in sheets, but one patch of air stayed dry. In that dry place stood a shape too thin to be a man and too tall to be a child. It held the lamb under one long arm. Its head bent sideways when it saw us, like a

hinge thinking.

I reached for my spear.

"No iron," Widow Fen said. "It is only borrowing."

"It can borrow my spear."

"Then it will return it inside you."

She took the cord from my hand and pulled the seventh knot loose with her teeth. The wind changed at once. Not strongly. Precisely. Rain swept sideways through the palisade gap and struck the dry patch. The thin thing hissed like a wet coal.

The lamb dropped into the mud and bolted.

The thing knocked on the empty air.

Three taps.

Every door in the village answered.

I heard latches jump, bars rattle, shutters bang. From the square came shouting. From Dobb's house came one heroic scream that I later learned was Dobb himself hiding under a table.

Widow Fen tied the seventh knot again.

The answering stopped.

The thin thing bowed, if a hinge can bow, and stepped backward into the rain until the rain had nothing left to fall around.

Afterward, Fletcher Dobb demanded the widow be punished for endangering his lamb. The lamb was standing beside him at the time eating his sleeve. I told Dobb the official finding was that no theft of wind had occurred, but that all washing lines should be secured against weather and foolishness.

He was not satisfied.

No one ever is.

I returned to Widow Fen's cottage before dusk. The cord hung over her door again. Nine knots. I asked what the eighth and ninth were for.

She gave me a biscuit.

"Captain," she said, "a village sleeps better when it does not know every door in the dark."

I have filed the cord as a lawful weather precaution.

I have also ordered the palisade repaired.
